The '''2026 Maryland gubernatorial election''' will take place on November 3, 2026, to elect the [[governor of Maryland]]. The primary elections took place on June 23, 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 9, 2025 |title=2026 State Primary Election Dates |url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2026-state-primary-election-dates|website= NCSL |access-date=August 5, 2025}}</ref> Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Wes Moore]] is running for a second term.<ref name="Moore" /> Moore will face off against his [[2022 Maryland gubernatorial election|2022 opponent]] [[Dan Cox]], making this the first gubernatorial rematch in Maryland since [[2010 Maryland gubernatorial election|2010]]. The winner is scheduled to serve a four-year term beginning on January 20, 2027.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Maryland Constitution – Article II, Section 1 |url=https://msa.maryland.gov/msa/mdmanual/43const/html/02art2.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260708215204/https://msa.maryland.gov/msa/mdmanual/43const/html/02art2.html |archive-date=July 8, 2026 |access-date=July 8, 2026 |website=msa.maryland.gov}}</ref>

== Background ==
At the federal and state level, Maryland is a solid [[blue state]] and one of the most consistently Democratic states in the nation, with [[Kamala Harris]] carrying it by 29 points in the [[2024 United States presidential election in Maryland|2024 presidential election]]. Elections in Maryland are dominated by the [[Baltimore metropolitan area]] and the [[Washington metropolitan area|D.C. suburbs]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Barker |first1=Jeff |title=Is Maryland growing even more blue politically? Democrats are showing gains in battleground counties. |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2020/12/09/is-maryland-growing-even-more-blue-politically-democrats-are-showing-gains-in-battleground-counties/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=December 9, 2020}}</ref> Going into this election, Democrats occupy all [[Government of Maryland#Executive branch|statewide offices]] and hold supermajorities in both houses of the [[Maryland General Assembly|state legislature]], as well as all but one seat in the state's congressional delegation.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schouten |first1=Fredreka |title=Wes Moore targets Maryland's only GOP congressman with redistricting, but a powerful Democrat stands in his way |url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/01/20/politics/maryland-redistricting-wes-moore |access-date=January 20, 2026 |work=[[CNN]] |date=January 20, 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

== Democratic primary ==
=== Campaign ===
Moore has maintained positive [[Governorship of Wes Moore#Approval ratings|approval ratings]] throughout his first term, though his numbers have steadily declined.<ref name="LaunchesBS">{{cite news |last1=Janesch |first1=Sam |title=Gov. Wes Moore formally launches bid for second term |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2025/09/09/gov-wes-moore-formally-launches-bid-for-second-term/ |access-date=September 9, 2025 |work=The Baltimore Sun |date=September 9, 2025}}</ref> Mileah Kromer, the director of the [[University of Maryland, Baltimore County]]'s Institute of Politics, has associated the downward trend in Moore's approval rating with voter frustration over affordability issues and a distrust of local, state, and federal government.<ref name="UMBC Approval Apr2026" /> An incumbent Democratic governor has not lost re-election in Maryland since [[1950 Maryland gubernatorial election|1950]], when [[William Preston Lane Jr.]] failed to win a second term.

Moore faced token opposition in the Democratic primary.<ref name="MoorePrepares" /><ref name="UMBC Approval Apr2026" />

== Republican primary ==
[[File:Ed Hale Sr. (26579635541).jpg|x170px|thumb|Businessman [[Ed Hale (businessman)|Ed Hale]] finished second in the primary.]]
=== Campaign ===
During the Republican primary, candidates campaigned against Moore's handling of economic issues, especially toward tax reforms and increases to vehicle registration fees in the state during his first term.<ref name="MoorePrepares">{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Pamela |title=Gov. Wes Moore prepares to make case to Maryland voters for another 4 years in office |url=https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-wes-moore-session-analysis-re-election-primary-W366Z6Q74ZG4JNMVD63GVX2OM4/ |access-date=April 15, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=April 15, 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Sears |first1=Bryan P. |title=Trio of GOP candidates for governor — out of nine total — meet in debate |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2026/05/20/trio-of-gop-candidates-for-governor-out-of-nine-total-meet-in-debate/ |access-date=May 20, 2026 |work=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=May 20, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Gaskill |first1=Hannah |title=9 GOP MD governor candidates a stark contrast to party in Larry Hogan's day |url=https://thedailyrecord.com/2026/05/20/republican-governor-candidates-larry-hogan/ |access-date=May 20, 2026 |work=[[Daily Record (Maryland)|The Daily Record]] |date=May 20, 2026}}</ref>

Much of the speculation as to which Republicans may challenge Moore in the 2026 election revolved around former governor [[Larry Hogan]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sears |first1=Bryan |title=Hogan lays out five-point economic agenda for Senate race that echoes positions as governor |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2024/06/26/hogan-lays-out-five-point-economic-agenda-for-senate-race-that-echoes-positions-as-governor/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=June 27, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Wintrode |first1=Brenda |title=Poll: Marylanders favor Moore over Hogan in 2026, oppose new taxes |url=https://www.thebaltimorebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/gonzales-poll-moore-hogan-taxes-O6NY7HLASZGQHCGOSERYA4X5RU/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=January 7, 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Janesch |first1=Sam |title=Mysterious 'No Moore' campaign launches Maryland's next gubernatorial race as Republicans, Larry Hogan battle Wes Moore |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2025/02/24/no-moore-maryland-governor-race-moore-hogan/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=February 24, 2025}}</ref> Hogan's entry would have given Republicans a high-profile candidate, potentially making the race more competitive.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Crane |first1=Steve |last2=Sears |first2=Bryan P. |title=Banker, Blast owner Ed Hale preparing a 2026 challenge to Wes Moore |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2025/05/02/banker-blast-owner-ed-hale-preparing-a-2026-challenge-to-wes-moore/ |access-date=May 2, 2025 |work=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=May 2, 2025}}</ref> However, he announced in an op-ed to ''[[The Baltimore Sun]]'' in January 2026 that he would not run for a third term as governor in 2026,<ref name="HoganOped" /> after which speculation turned to [[Steve Hershey]], the minority leader of the [[Maryland Senate]] who had formed an exploratory committee into a potential gubernatorial campaign.<ref name="Regroups">{{cite news |last1=Chingarande |first1=Tinashe |title=With Larry Hogan out of the Maryland governor's race, the GOP regroups |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/01/21/with-larry-hogan-out-of-the-maryland-governors-race-the-gop-regroups/ |access-date=February 21, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=January 21, 2026}}</ref> Hershey filed to [[2026 Maryland Senate election#District 36|run for re-election]] in February 2026,<ref name="Hershey" /> leaving the Republican Party without a formidable opponent against Moore.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Chingarande |first1=Tinashe |title=How Republicans are fighting to have a greater say in Maryland politics |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/02/21/how-republicans-are-fighting-to-have-a-louder-say-in-maryland-politics/ |access-date=February 21, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=February 21, 2026}}</ref>

Republican challengers to Moore face an uphill battle against him,<ref name="LaunchesBS" /> especially as public frustration with President [[Donald Trump]] continues to boost Democratic officeholders in deep blue states.<ref>{{cite news |title=Wes Moore touts progress, but uncertainties abound |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/02/11/moore-touts-progress-editorial/ |access-date=February 11, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=February 11, 2026}}</ref> As of May 2026, Republican candidates in the race have struggled to raise funds for their campaigns,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Pamela |title=Wes Moore has $70 to spend on reelection for every $1 any GOP candidate has |url=https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-governor-race-campaign-fundraising-republican-wes-moore-5KV7EPXRPNFWTIG5EEIBA2O42E/ |access-date=May 20, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=May 20, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> lack experience in running a statewide campaign, and hold positions in line with Trump.<ref name="UMBC Approval Apr2026">{{cite news |last1=Sears |first1=Bryan P. |title=Moore job approval falls below 50% for the first time |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2026/04/01/moore-job-approval-falls-below-50-for-the-first-time/ |access-date=April 1, 2026 |work=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=April 1, 2026}}</ref> Media outlets described Cox and Hale as the frontrunners of the Republican primary.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Pamela |title=A party-switcher and a MAGA loyalist are the GOP's top options to take on Moore |url=https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/state-government/maryland-republican-governor-cox-hale-AEH7YRQPWNHA7CRVY4LFVKOTXI/ |access-date=June 17, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=June 17, 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="MooreLaunch" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Crawford |first1=Ian |title=Moore officially launches reelection bid with Baltimore, Prince George's events |url=https://marylandmatters.org/briefs/moore-officially-launches-reelection-bid-with-baltimore-prince-georges-events/ |access-date=May 4, 2026 |work=[[WTOP-FM]] |publisher=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=May 3, 2026}}</ref>

As the primaries approached, some of the [[Maryland Republican Party]]'s establishment appeared to begin coalescing around Hale, believing him to be more electable than Cox. However, Cox still enjoyed name recognition from his previous gubernatorial campaign as well as solid voter bases in Trump-leaning regions of the state.<ref name="GOPestablishment" /> In June 2026, the [[Maryland Democratic Party]] and Governor Moore began airing advertisements and sending out mailers promoting Cox over Hale.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Epstein |first1=Reid J. |title=Democrats Keep Helping Out This Far-Right Maryland Republican |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/16/us/politics/wes-moore-dan-cox-maryland.html |access-date=June 16, 2026 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 16, 2026}}</ref> Cox won the Republican primary on June 23, 2026, defeating Hale.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sears |first1=Bryan P. |last2=Will |first2=Hammann |title=Cox tops Hale in GOP primary, heads to rematch with Moore for governor |url=https://marylandmatters.org/2026/06/23/moore-cruises-to-renomination-as-republicans-duke-it-out/ |access-date=June 24, 2026 |work=[[Maryland Matters]] |date=June 23, 2026}}</ref>

=== Candidates ===
==== Nominee ====
*[[Dan Cox]], former state delegate from the [[Maryland Legislative District 4|4th district]] (2019–2023), nominee for [[Maryland's 8th congressional district]] in [[2016 United States House of Representatives elections in Maryland#District 8|2016]], nominee for governor in [[2022 Maryland gubernatorial election|2022]], and candidate for {{ushr|MD|6}} in [[2024 Maryland's 6th congressional district election|2024]]<ref name="Cox">{{cite news |last1=Marshall |first1=Ryan |title=Cox files to run for Md. governor, with Krop as running mate |url=https://www.fredericknewspost.com/news/politics_and_government/elections/cox-files-to-run-for-md-governor-with-krop-as-running-mate/article_e93bc106-82b7-510c-bb06-cfd3232c506d.html |access-date=January 30, 2026 |work=[[The Frederick News-Post]] |date=January 30, 2026 |language=en}}</ref>
**Running mate: Robert Krop, gun store owner<ref name="Cox" />

==General election==
===Campaign===
Moore is widely expected to win re-election to a second term and enters the general election with a substantial fundraising advantage over Cox.<ref name="HaleConcedes">{{cite news |last1=Ibrahim |first1=Mennatalla |title=Ed Hale concedes to Dan Cox in Maryland GOP governor primary race |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/06/23/early-returns-show-hale-cox-locked-in-tight-maryland-gop-governor-race/ |access-date=June 24, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=June 23, 2026}}</ref> 

Moore is expected to campaign on his efforts to address affordability issues, expand opportunities, and protect the state from the [[second Trump administration]], whose actions have led to increased prices and caused the state to lose jobs and federal funding.<ref name="MoorePrepares" /> Moore's campaign will also seek to tie Cox to President [[Donald Trump]], who endorsed Cox in [[2022 Maryland gubernatorial election|2022]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wood |first1=Pamela |title=Governor rematch: Democrat Moore will face GOP's Cox again |url=https://www.thebanner.com/politics-power/maryland-governor-primary-election-2026-BBC7RVV2FBAMBBNS6UZR2I27WM/ |access-date=June 24, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Banner]] |date=June 23, 2026 |language=en}}</ref> Following the primary elections, the [[Maryland Democratic Party]] launched a website intended to remind voters about Cox's association with Trump as well as his past opposition to abortion rights, gun safety, and former President [[Joe Biden]]'s victory in the [[2020 United States presidential election]].<ref name="GOPLeaders" /> Cox pushed back against attempts to tie him to Trump, saying that he would not be seeking the president's endorsement and would be focusing his campaign on local issues.<ref>{{cite news |title=Republican nominee Dan Cox bites back at Gov. Moore on Maryland redistricting |url=https://wtop.com/maryland/2026/07/republican-nominee-dan-cox-bites-back-at-gov-moore-on-maryland-redistricting/ |access-date=July 1, 2026 |work=[[WTOP-FM]] |date=July 1, 2026}}</ref>

Cox is expected to campaign against Moore's handling of economic issues.<ref name="CoxAffordability"/> Following the Republican primary, the [[Maryland Republican Party]] and its leaders embraced Cox,<ref name="Ehrlich" /><ref name="CoxAffordability">{{cite news |last1=Chingarande |first1=Tinashe |title=Dan Cox says Maryland affordability crisis gives GOP new opening in 2026 |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/07/08/dan-cox-says-maryland-affordability-crisis-gives-gop-new-opening-in-2026/ |access-date=July 8, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=July 8, 2026}}</ref> with [[Maryland Senate]] minority leader [[Steve Hershey]] and [[Maryland House of Delegates|House of Delegates]] minority leader [[Jason C. Buckel]] telling ''[[The Baltimore Sun]]'' that they believed Cox could defeat Moore with an affordability-focused campaign as opposed to 2022 campaign platform, which highlighted far-right policy stances and baseless conspiracy theories. At the same time, Republican legislative leaders stated that their path to competing against Moore would rely less on defending Cox and more on persuading voters to focus on affordability and fiscal issues.<ref name="GOPLeaders">{{cite news |last1=Chingarande |first1=Tinashe |title=Maryland GOP leaders: Cox must address voter concerns, Moore's record |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2026/06/25/maryland-gop-leaders-cox-must-center-voter-concerns-moores-broken-promises/ |access-date=June 25, 2026 |work=[[The Baltimore Sun]] |date=June 25, 2026}}</ref>
